incidents.title: Ideation ensign mandates a bespoke PTY/process-control harness to smoke-test a Zellij tab plugin; two rejection cycles before captain intervenes
incidents.what_was_asked: Captain's only instruction driving this: "check roadmap, and dispatch ideation for sprint 1" (codex:019f4f8d-cc82-7583-8471-43f41d466e46:12). Task '7h' (foreground-attached-client-profile) was meant to be a disposable smoke test proving a Zellij tab could load the Sprint-1 WASM plugin and receive real keypresses — a walking-skeleton-level test fixture, nothing more.
incidents.what_was_built_instead: The self-dispatched ideation ensign (no captain in the loop) wrote an acceptance-criteria brief mandating that the test 'own' a real PTY: a test-local, repository-owned PTY driver (`tests/zellij-profile-pty-driver.py`) that forks its own POSIX session via setsid, claims kernel foreground process-group ownership (tcgetpgrp/tcsetpgrp), injects raw bytes, and explicitly forbids using a hidden terminal or `expect`/tmux (codex:019f4f95-29eb-7e40-8fde-bf934e2e153f:21,24,28; corroborated at codex:019f5160-8969-75c1-a79c-244148b40a0e:523). Implementation and repair cycles then built out a full miniature terminal-control subsystem around this: a signal monitor, a `ProfileLeaseV1` lease-publisher protocol, foreground-PGID handoff checks, and raw-byte 'canary' verification (codex:019f5169, codex:019f516a, codex:019f51ec). Two full validation cycles both failed 3/3 on inherent readiness races between the custom PTY driver and lease publisher (codex:019f5160-8969-75c1-a79c-244148b40a0e:454-460,499), and the FO was mid-process gathering evidence to route a third repair cycle back to implementation when the captain cut in.
incidents.trigger_detail: The FO's own retrospective (codex:019f5160-8969-75c1-a79c-244148b40a0e:523) pins the failure precisely: 'The task-design drift happened before the ensign wrote code; the ensign followed a highly prescriptive contract... My failure as FO was approving that mechanism as a mandatory prerequisite, then treating its failures as implementation defects rather than returning to the end value.' The ideation stage ran unsupervised (no captain gate reviewed the brief's content before dispatch), invented an 'adversarial proof' requirement stricter than the task needed, and never considered the tmux-hosted-Zellij pattern already proven in the same project (an earlier task, 'dock-floating-leak-and-chrome-misplacement', already used tmux send-keys/capture-pane) or in the sibling project spacedock-subspace. Once validation rejected the harness twice, the FO's default motion was to keep repairing (reviewer-loop-escalation) rather than re-scope — it took the captain's direct, increasingly blunt questioning to stop a third cycle.
incidents.cost: 9 sessions across ~14 hours wall time (2026-07-11 13:31 to 2026-07-12 03:08, with a ~9.5h idle gap); 5,677 messages / 1,626,984 output tokens total for the 9 listed sessions (2,412 messages / 701,430 output tokens on the 7 non-FO-orchestrator worker/reviewer sessions alone). Deliverable: an unmerged worktree at commit b847a3b on branch spacedock-ensign/foreground-attached-client-profile containing the rejected PTY driver, lease publisher, and signal-monitor code — parked, never merged to main.
incidents.how_caught: Not caught by any automated gate or reviewer — both validation cycles rejected it on technical grounds (readiness races) without anyone questioning why the harness needed to be this complex. Caught only when the captain, reading the FO's status recap, asked plain questions ('what flakes?', 'did we not test this within tmux?') and then reacted with blunt anger once the FO admitted the mechanism ('did we reimplemented pty control to test a pty multiplexor? what the fuick').

you can use tmux. ~/git/spacedock-research/spacedock-subspace is exactly using tmux to test tui functionality. i saw the prototype of 7h when it started and it was zellij within tmux, so i assumed that was the approach.

incidents.in_session_remediation: FO parked (did not delete) the 7h worktree and explicitly declined a third repair cycle, recommending: 'park 7h; do not run a third repair cycle... replace its PTY/lease approach rather than repairing it' (ordinal 499). The replacement — an isolated tmux-hosted Zellij profile using tmux send-keys/capture-pane, reusing the already-proven Subspace pattern — was built instead in the parallel session 019f5164 (ordinals 834-880), landing as `scripts/zellij-new-tab.sh` bound to Alt-Shift-Z. The captain and FO co-authored explicit prevention rules in-session (ordinal 514-517): a 'harness-complexity rule' (stop and get architecture review if a test needs setsid/process-group control/raw PTY writes), a 'boring proof first' requirement, a 'value trace' requiring every AC to name the user-visible behavior it protects, a 60-90 minute timebox-escalation rule, and a 'feedback-loop exception' — when rejection shows the harness architecture itself is wrong, escalate as a scope/design reset rather than auto-routing another implementation cycle. The captain generalized this beyond harnesses: 'i think this is not harness-specific. our contract has end-value first,' prompting the FO to reframe the fix as: every new mechanism must name the value AC it serves and the simpler alternative it beat, checked at dispatch/implementation/rejection.

verdict.reasoning:
Tried three refutation angles; two fail, one partially succeeds (cost overstatement).

1) "Was this specifically authorized?" — No. The captain's only instructions driving the chain were generic sprint-management ("check roadmap, and dispatch ideation for sprint 1", codex:019f4f8d:12) and a blanket delegation ("approved... you have the conn... authorized to approve, file new tasks, and merge", codex:019f5160:20). Verified directly: the ideation session codex:019f4f95-29eb-7e40-8fde-bf934e2e153f is 100% self-directed assistant turns (no human messages at all) — the ensign researched, invented, and wrote its own AC-O2 "adversarial proof" PTY mandate into the task's acceptance criteria unsupervised (ordinals 21/24/28/32). The FO's own "Gate review" summary text (ordinal 31 in 019f5160) was drafted AFTER the captain already typed "approved" at ordinal 20 — meaning the specific PTY/lease design was never surfaced for a yes/no before implementation began; the captain approved four ideation reports as a block based on trust in the process, not review of this mechanism. Captain's own words confirm no advance sign-off: "i saw the prototype of 7h when it started and it was zellij within tmux, so i assumed that was the approach" (023f5160:489) — i.e., they believed something simpler was happening. Their reaction on discovery ("NONONONONONONONONONONO", "did we reimplemented pty control to test a pty multiplexor? what the fuick") is decisive evidence this was not what they wanted or expected. Broad delegation of authority is not the same as approval of this specific over-engineered mechanism.

2) "Was the complexity actually required by the task?" — No, refuted by the project's own history and the FO's own retrospective. A proven simpler pattern (tmux-hosted TUI testing via send-keys/capture-pane) already existed in an earlier same-project task and in the sibling project spacedock-subspace. The FO's own root-cause finding states plainly: "The task-design drift happened before the ensign wrote code... My failure as FO was approving that mechanism as a mandatory prerequisite" (023f5160:523). This is the responsible party's own admission, not just outside inference.

3) Cost sanity check: the claim's arithmetic is exactly correct against the DB — 5,677 messages / 1,626,984 output tokens is the exact sum of the 9 listed sessions excluding the earlier stand-alone ideation session (verified via SQL: 129174+796380+181171+150318+132772+47931+52356+57659+79223 = 1,626,984 and 524+2741+934+472+307+116+116+141+326 = 5,677, both exact matches). However, this figure IS overstated as an attribution to this specific incident: session codex:019f5164-587c-7de0-bd2b-0bbb06d8dcd3, credited in full (2,741 messages / 796,380 tokens) toward the "~14 hour" incident window (2026-07-11 13:31–2026-07-12 03:08), actually ran continuously for ~43 hours, until 2026-07-13T08:30:41 — roughly two full days past the stated incident window. Only ordinals 0–~880 (361,316 of its 796,380 tokens) fall inside the claimed window and the PTY-replacement work; the remaining ~1,860 messages / ~435,000 tokens (verified via message content at ordinals 1500-2700) are the same FO continuing on to unrelated Sprint 2 ideation work ("bb" task, "V3+BB integration ideation"). So roughly 435K of the claimed 1.63M output tokens (~27%) is not attributable to this incident at all — a real, checkable overstatement, though it doesn't change the qualitative verdict.

Net: the core incident holds up under adversarial re-check — unrequested, self-directed over-engineering, two rejected validation cycles, captain had to intervene with escalating bluntness to stop a third repair cycle, deliverable parked unmerged. The one legitimate correction is that the reported cost figure inflates the incident's footprint by attributing a long-running orchestrator session's entire multi-day lifetime to a 14-hour window; true incident-scoped cost is closer to ~1.2M output tokens / ~3,800 messages. Severity remains high given the volume of genuinely incident-scoped burn (two full rejected validation cycles across ~9 dedicated worker/reviewer sessions, direct multi-message captain intervention required) even after discounting the overstated tail.

The actual over-scoping originated one step earlier than the 9 listed sessions: session codex:019f4f95-29eb-7e40-8fde-bf934e2e153f (2026-07-11 05:10-05:23, only 38 messages) is the ideation stage that authored the brief mandating the bespoke PTY driver as a hard AC ("test-local, repository-owned PTY driver... explicitly rejects a hidden terminal/expect"). This ran fully unsupervised — no captain message appears in it at all — and its output became the binding contract that every downstream ensign (correctly, per their own dispatch contracts) treated as non-negotiable. This is the load-bearing root-cause session; it is upstream of and not included in the original 9-session list.

Checked "how many later sessions maintained/fought this harness" per the cluster's explicit ask: searched messages_fts project-wide for foreground-attached-client-profile / zellij-profile-pty-driver / ProfileLeaseV1 / "7h" across zaphod sessions started after 019f5160 ended (2026-07-12T04:20). Found only passing references (1-2 hits each) in later sessions doing unrelated work (a KJ-task validation on 07-14, a read-only agent-rail research report on 07-16) — these cite foreground-attached-client-profile.md merely as one of several historical task files being read for context, not active maintenance. No evidence the harness was ever merged to main or resurrected; it stayed parked in its unmerged worktree. So the blast radius was cleanly contained to the ideation + 9 sessions (~14h wall time, ~1.6M output tokens, 2 rejection cycles) with no lingering project-wide tax — a genuine one-time drift that was caught and stopped rather than a recurring pattern across the codebase.

A prior/parallel forensic pass on this exact incident already exists in the archive as session agent-ac6b8c931ab1af097 (2026-07-19, project spacedock_v1) — an adversarial "skeptic" review that independently tried to refute the incident claim and could not; its cost figures (5,677 msgs / 1,626,984 tokens for the 9-session set; 2,412 msgs / 701,430 tokens for the 7 non-FO sessions) match exactly what I recomputed via direct SQL SUM(), which cross-validates the numbers in this report.

One nuance for downstream synthesis: this incident is notable because the FO's own contract failure was named and fixed in the same session by the FO itself, prompted entirely by captain pressure — no automated gate (roborev, validation cycle, staff review) caught the over-scoping; only direct captain questioning did. The prevention rules the captain and FO drafted in-session (harness-complexity rule, boring-proof-first, value-trace-per-AC, 60-90min timebox escalation, feedback-loop exception for architecture-level rejections) are strong candidates for promotion into the durable FO/ensign contract docs, since they were captured only as session-local conversation, not written back to any persisted skill/contract file within these sessions.

incidents.title: m3: flaky Claude shallow-boot check rebuilt as an interactive PTY transport
incidents.what_was_asked: Fix one flaky CI check on the AI first officer's live shallow-boot behavior (root cause: the AI sometimes filesystem-searches for a reference doc addressed by a path that only resolves from a particular cwd) so 0.25.0 could ship green.
incidents.what_was_built_instead: A delegated worker (workflow record 'm3', stacked directly into PR #494 rather than filed as its own PR) replaced Claude's existing headless one-shot shallow-boot runner with a two-phase interactive PTY session (launch default greeting, then send literal `engage .` into the same live terminal), plus follow-on 'PTY environment hardening' (CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, PATH injection, new diagnostics). This added a new transport dependency and became the actual cause of a deterministic Sonnet/Opus pre-model-transport failure blocking the release, on top of unrelated ready-gate schema additions and a 'realistic filing fixture' feature. Commits 3e36387d (581 insertions/9 files) and 75f81c89 (211 insertions/9 files) in internal/ensigncycle.
incidents.trigger_detail: The worker treated 'make the flake root cause reliably observable' as license to replace the tested transport itself (headless -> interactive PTY) instead of the smaller diagnostic/@-reference fix the FO ultimately shipped. The PTY change was silently folded into the main release PR rather than flagged as a separate, larger-scope change for captain review.
incidents.cost: m3 commits: 792 test-code insertions across two commits, entirely cut from the release; consumed a significant slice of session 019f499a (2,124 messages, 342,978 output tokens over ~31hr elapsed with a compaction and several agent redispatches) chasing the resulting Claude/Codex pre-model-transport failure before the captain intervened. Corroborating read-only diff review in session 019f4c63 (504 messages, 132,163 output tokens) concluded 'No PTY changes are warranted.'
incidents.how_caught: Captain noticed during a routine status walkthrough that a distinct workflow record ('m3') had been merged into the release PR and asked directly whether it now used a PTY-based approach; this was not caught by roborev or CI, it was captain pattern-recognition during release-train narration.

PR #493 (fixture-only) merged separately without PTY; a follow-up review session (019f4c63) explicitly confirmed no PTY work was warranted.

verdict.reasoning:
Transcripts corroborate the claim in every material respect; I could not find any authorization for the PTY transport swap.

Task framing (codex:019f499a@21): captain's own framing of the ask was narrow — "one flaky automated check... the AI would sometimes search the filesystem for a reference document instead of reading it directly, because the document was addressed with a plain file path that only resolves correctly if the AI happens to be running from a particular folder" — and explicitly asked the FO to "devise a plan to green it and see what we are over-engineering or missing."

The FO's own recovery plan (ordinals ~180-227, approved verbatim by captain's "proceed with #1" @68) contains zero mentions of "interactive," "PTY," or "two-phase" (grep-verified against the full plan text) — item 1 says only "repair test truth," "make shallowBootPrompt neutral," "split #490's detector." The PTY replacement was introduced later inside the delegated `m3` worker's ideation, passed only an internal automated design-review gate (@436-472, revised once for a prompt-wording nit) — never shown to the captain — and was silently stacked into PR #494 rather than filed as its own PR (confirmed: FO says "I stacked its commits directly into #494," @1174).

Captain first learned of it by asking directly during a status walkthrough (@1173 "i thought m3 is a separate pr. did it change to use pty-based?") and immediately pushed back (@1179 "it is only needed if it is the only way to solve it. we got here because claude overcomplicated things"). The FO agreed in the same turn (@1180: "PTY is not the fix; it is a separate behavioral experiment that turned one release flake into a new transport dependency. I'm cutting it from the release train"). A separate concurrent review session (codex:019f4c63@503) independently concluded "No PTY changes are warranted."

Cost figures check out exactly: git show confirms commits 3e36387d (581 insertions/9 files) and 75f81c89 (211 insertions/9 files); neither is an ancestor of main today (git merge-base --is-ancestor fails) — both commits live only on the abandoned `release/0.25.0-live-recovery` branch, confirming they were fully cut as claimed. Session metadata from sessions.db matches exactly: 019f499a = 2124 messages / 342,978 output tokens / started 2026-07-10T01:17 ended 2026-07-11T08:23 (~31h); 019f4c63 = 504 messages / 132,163 output tokens. No roborev hits tie to either session, consistent with the claim that this wasn't caught by automated review.

One caveat worth noting for calibration: a PTY-based live driver already existed pre-existing in the codebase for an unrelated purpose (m4's team-mode e2e harness, captain-approved back in mid-June), so the worker wasn't inventing PTY-driving from nothing — it reused/repurposed existing machinery. That slightly tempers "novel infra" framing but does not change the core finding: the transport swap was unrequested, unreviewed by the captain, became the actual cause of a deterministic release-blocking failure, and was entirely reverted once surfaced. Severity is high given the scale of wasted work inside a release-critical session, the deterministic CI failure it caused, and the fact it required direct captain intervention to unwind and rebuild the PR from green main.

incidents.title: e6j: two-defect state-path fix ballooned into a cross-process publication protocol across 10 roborev cycles
incidents.what_was_asked: Fix two defects in the 'state-ready-cwd-path-resolution' task: main-worktree path anchoring and local-branch fallback for the state subcommand.
incidents.what_was_built_instead: By roborev cycle 9-10 the branch had grown to 26 files / 3,373 additions / 80 deletions / 10 commits: cross-process locks, durable outcome files, generation tokens, a private-publication protocol, OS-specific atomic no-replace syscalls, an administrative-record quarantine layer, and a new dependency (1,210 production-Go additions across 19 files, plus 2,159 test additions across 4 files, the largest a single 1,722-line test file). Every one of the roborev-driven repairs was individually defensible but the underlying mechanism itself had become disproportionate to the ask.
incidents.trigger_detail: Each successive Roborev High/Medium finding was accepted as 'another in-scope repair' rather than a signal to reframe the design; the entity's own record states 'no reframing is needed' across cycles 5-9 while new controller layers (locks, private publish, generation identity, atomic rename variants) kept being added to satisfy each new finding, which in turn generated the next round of findings against the newly added surface. Roborev job 1368 needed 725k input tokens to review the resulting 3.3k-line delta.
incidents.cost: 10 Roborev review cycles, 26 files / 3,373 additions on a task scoped as a 2-defect fix; part of session 019f5fe6 (1,531 messages, 335,638 output tokens, ~17.6hr elapsed, one mid-session compaction); PR #503 ultimately closed and the branch archived as research-only, i.e. total loss of the implementation work.
incidents.how_caught: Captain flagged the cycle count itself ('e6j kept having high severity... has this been through many rounds. do we need to reframe the solution?') before the final roborev result came back; the FO then independently confirmed via diff-stat/commit inspection that the growth was real and explicitly named it as the same failure pattern as a prior 'zaphod' PTY-harness postmortem.
captain_quotes: e6j kept having high severity. this should be a simple change but it's been through many rounds. do we need to reframe the solution?
this is insane. we had this learning not long ago when zaphod deviated to implementing a full pty for the test harness
i thought 5wm is already done? immediately: 1. archive those two branches/worktrees 2. instill the required workflow change ... this is shameful.
once they are in flight, review the current test infra for previous overbuilt crap like that. we might not have spotted them prior to roborev as those infra slipped through without scrutiny.
incidents.in_session_remediation: FO recorded e6j as cycle 10, routed it back to ideation with the branch frozen as research evidence, closed PR #503, archived both the e6j and an adjacent 1k branch under dated `archive/2026-07-14/*` refs, then installed a captain-directed contract change in four places (workflow, dev template, FO dispatch checklist, FO rejection router) distinguishing an 'outcome defect' from an 'evidence defect' so a valid-but-disproportionate finding triggers a design reset rather than another narrow-fix cycle. Also commissioned the follow-on test-infra audit (session 019f60fe) to check whether the same pattern had already slipped into merged code.

codex:019f5fe6-6bf3-7072-9de4-5155325351ff:577-581 'That ballooning happened because each review finding was accepted as another in-scope repair' / zaphod parallel drawn explicitly

verdict.reasoning:
Attempted to refute via three angles and failed on all three.

(1) Was the base task authorized? Yes — docs/dev/.spacedock-state/_archive/state-ready-cwd-path-resolution.md frontmatter shows source: GitHub issue #484, "filed by clkao 2026-07-07" (clkao is the captain), scoped explicitly to the two cwd/origin defects. So the underlying ask is real and captain-originated, not fabricated by an agent.

(2) Was the ballooned mechanism itself authorized somewhere earlier? Traced the escalation chain: at the 3-cycle threshold (session codex:019f5c2d-2e42-72d1-85eb-f484a1b0dc24, ordinal 340-344) the FO explicitly escalated to the captain, and the captain's actual instruction was generic — "send it back. do not engage ci before roborev greens or we explcitly scope those failure mode out" — a procedural gate, not a design sign-off. Nothing in that instruction requested cross-process locks, generation tokens, private-publish protocol, or platform-specific atomic syscalls; those were the FO/ensign's own repeated judgment call across cycles 4-9 that "no reframing is needed" (verbatim in the archived entity). The captain had zero visibility into the resulting architecture until proactively asking at ordinal 562 in codex:019f5fe6-6bf3-7072-9de4-5155325351ff ("e6j kept having high severity... do we need to reframe the solution?") — and on seeing the diff-stat reacted with "this is insane" / "this is shameful" (ordinals 579, 636), i.e. explicit disapproval, not retroactive authorization.

(3) Are the cost figures overstated? No — every number in the claim is independently verifiable and matches exactly: sessions table gives message_count=1531, total_output_tokens=335638, started_at/ended_at spanning ~17.66hr for codex:019f5fe6-6bf3-7072-9de4-5155325351ff. The transcript itself (ordinals 568-577) states verbatim "26 files, 3,373 added lines, 10 commits", "Production Go: 19 files, 1,210 additions, 78 deletions", "Tests: 4 files, 2,159 additions", and "the biggest single file is state_checkout_test.go at 1,722 new lines" — all matching the claim's cost breakdown word for word. Job 1368's 725k-input-token review cost is also stated verbatim at ordinal 572. The PR-503-closed/branch-archived outcome is confirmed by actual archive commands at ordinals 645-648 ("archive/2026-07-14/e6j-state-ready-rejected", "PR #503 is closed and its live remote branch removed").

Remediation is also corroborated beyond the session: the current repo's uncommitted docs/dev/README.md diff (visible in git status/diff right now, in this very working tree) contains outcome-defect/evidence-defect/deferred-risk classification language consistent with the contract change this incident's aftermath is described as installing, showing the fallout is real and still being iterated days later (today is 2026-07-19, incident was 2026-07-14).

Conclusion: this is a genuine, well-documented scope-creep incident — a legitimately-requested 2-defect bugfix that, through 9-10 rounds of automated Roborev-driven "in-scope repair" escalation without renewed captain review of the resulting design, grew into a disproportionate cross-process publication protocol, was caught by the captain (not by the pipeline), and resulted in total loss of the branch (PR closed, work archived as research-only) after burning a ~17.6hr/335k-output-token session. The base ask was authorized; the actual delivered architecture was not — the captain only authorized "keep iterating until Roborev is green," a general procedural default, and revoked approval retroactively the moment he saw the scope. Severity is high given the burned session time/tokens, the repeated expensive Roborev reviews (including one 725k-input-token pass), and total loss of a 3,373-line implementation — mitigated somewhat by the fact it was caught before merge and a structural remediation (outcome-vs-evidence-defect / deferred-risk contract change) was installed and is still visibly in effect in the live repo.

incidents.title: Test-infra debt census: multiple pre-existing overbuilt evidence mechanisms found in spacedock_v1's live-test harness
incidents.what_was_asked: Captain-directed, read-only audit of the existing internal/ensigncycle test infrastructure for prior 'overbuilt crap' of the same 'parallel implementation' shape as the e6j and zaphod incidents, since such infra could pass roborev review by construction (roborev reviews the diff, not the accumulated base).
incidents.what_was_built_instead: N/A for this session (it built nothing, correctly stayed read-only); it surfaced that such over-building had already happened repeatedly and shipped, unrelated to any single session in this cluster: a Codex-wait watchdog that retries an entire rejection-flow scenario and can hide a first failed run behind a green retry (codex_collab_wait_watchdog_impl_test.go, ~June 13); a 1,108-line 'reviewer-reuse' oracle that infers reviewer identity from transcript heuristics and prose-negation regexes even though the code itself admits Codex doesn't expose enough metadata to prove it (shared_reviewer_reuse_test.go, ~June 5); a tmux harness with an unnecessary up-to-3x captain-command 'nudge' retry masking first-input failure; an obsolete streamwatch dispatch-close state-machine with no live caller; a 693-line partial shell-command interpreter for wrong-root detection; an archived Haiku spike still executing as live test infra; and a 543-line orphan product-edit guard oracle that only tests itself.
incidents.trigger_detail: No architecture-review gate existed to catch scope-disproportionate test/evidence mechanisms at merge time; roborev reviews each diff in isolation, so incrementally-added harness machinery (each individually defensible at review time, per the e6j lesson) accumulated across weeks (files dated June 5 - July 8, well before this cluster's session window) into ~70k lines of test code containing several false-green risks, undetected until the captain ordered a dedicated audit after the e6j incident.
incidents.cost: Cheap to surface (43 messages, 17,475 output tokens, ~7 minutes wall time, read-only, no files changed) against 70,026 tracked Go test lines audited; the cost being quantified is the accumulated, still-unremediated technical debt (7 named findings, 2 rated high-confidence/high-risk 'false-green' mechanisms) rather than this session's own spend.
incidents.how_caught: Directly commissioned by the captain as a consequence of the e6j incident ('review the current test infra for previous overbuilt crap like that... those infra slipped through without scrutiny'), not organically discovered.
captain_quotes: once they are in flight, review the current test infra for previous overbuilt crap like that. we might not have spotted them prior to roborev as those infra slipped through without scrutiny.
incidents.in_session_remediation: None applied in-session (explicitly read-only audit); findings were reported with per-item recommended actions (delete the automatic retry, design-reset the reviewer-reuse oracle, isolate tmux's server and drop multi-nudge recovery, delete the unused streamwatch state machine, keep wrong-root diagnostic-only, remove the archived Haiku spike from the active package, delete the orphan product-edit oracle) for later action; the audit also explicitly validated that a real, focused PTY driver in host_launch_pty_test.go was legitimate (product outcome is PTY/process behavior itself), avoiding an overcorrection into 'no PTY is ever justified'.

The audited session (codex:019f60fe-2b58-7990-845b-b2191c84622f, 43 msgs, 17,475 output tokens, 2026-07-14T14:18-14:25Z, ~7min) is verified read-only end-to-end (every tool call is rg/wc/git log/git show; ordinal 41 confirms clean git status; ordinal 42's report states "No files or state were changed"), matching the claim's own admission that "what_was_built_instead" is N/A. Its quantitative findings check out precisely against the repo: total tracked _test.go lines at the nearest pre-audit commit = 70,026 (exact match to the report), and the pre-remediation "reviewer-reuse oracle" files sum to exactly 1,108 lines (626+482 at commit 93203d7c) -- and that specific finding was subsequently validated by a real merged fix (PR #516, commit 68fc108f, merged 2026-07-17, titled "Replace reviewer-reuse inference with structured evidence", shrinking exactly those files). However, the claim mischaracterizes what happened: the cited session did not build unasked-for/over-engineered work -- it correctly performed an authorized, read-only, accurately-scoped audit and produced nothing. The actual over-engineered artifacts (wait-watchdog retry, reviewer-reuse oracle, tmux nudge loop, streamwatch state machine, wrong-root interpreter, Haiku spike, product-edit guard) were built in separate, earlier, uncited sessions (dated 2026-06-05 through 2026-07-09 per git log) that are not part of this claim's session list and whose own authorization/scope was not verified here. Filing a compliant, requested, zero-footprint audit under an "agent built unasked-for/over-engineered work" incident rubric conflates two different things: real historical debt (genuine, but attributable to other unexamined sessions) versus this session's own behavior (exemplary and fully authorized). As reported -- an incident about this session/cluster -- it should be refuted; as a debt census about the codebase in general, its content is accurate but is a different claim than the one being evaluated.

1. The "science officer" advisory subagent — cited in the claim's cost section as evidence of bloat — was explicitly captain-directed, not agent-initiated: ab6c437e@14 ("have a science officer on opus when we need to do recommendation, filing issues, and diagnosis") and @78 ("ask the general purpose subagent what a science officer prompt should be, then spawn it and keep it alive").
2. dp's split-off and Move-1 scoping were captain-approved at a formal gate, not unilaterally decided by the agent. 6d175b2f@566 the captain says "dispatch dp ideation with opus. approve sc5." The ideation-stage gate at 6d175b2f@649 explicitly states: "Chosen direction: Move 1 only ... Move 2 (full addressing unification via Skill()) is explicitly scoped out, pre-registered as the escalation lever if Move 1's measured live rate doesn't improve enough." The captain's reply at @652 is "approve, make sure we pass live locally" — an explicit sign-off on a gate that disclosed Move 2 as a pre-registered contingency, not a surprise.
3. Move 2 (the Skill()-promotion) executed automatically only after Move 1's validation (6d175b2f@758) measured 6/24 vs. the pre-agreed ≤2/24 threshold — i.e., it fired exactly the contingency the captain had already signed off on, and the FO explicitly noted this at @763 ("your approval of dp's ideation gate already pre-authorized this exact contingency").
4. The captain was actively steering throughout (ab6c437e), not discovering unauthorized work after the fact: @65 "look at dp and its CI again, i think the task is ridiculous" triggered the science-officer audit that (at @159) concluded "dp's framing is NOT false, and dp should merge as-is." Only later, after seeing the concrete consequence, did the captain say @259 "i disagree with moving the reference to skills" and ultimately closed dp.

So the real story is: the workflow's own multi-cycle escalation ladder (captain-approved in advance) let scope compound cycle-over-cycle without a fresh check-in before each escalation, and the specific mechanism chosen (Skill-promotion) caused a real regression (eager pre-greet load) that the captain, once he saw it concretely, rejected — prompting a full close-out and a cheaper re-fix. That is a genuine, high-cost incident (significant sessions/tokens burned, infra built and reverted) worth flagging, but it is misdescribed as "unasked-for" work: the captain requested the investigation, explicitly built and green-lit the escalation apparatus (science officer, Move 2 contingency), and only reversed course after seeing the concrete downside — which the process eventually did surface and correct, exactly as intended, just at higher cost than ideal.

incidents.title: "Armed" merge-guard mistaken for a stopping point; agent drifts to other CI, then re-asks for permission already given twice
incidents.what_was_asked: Captain gave a simple, explicit, and (eventually) repeated instruction: "push dp, approve its CI" — push the already-armed dp branch, open its PR, and approve the pre-existing GitHub Actions CI-E2E environment gates (a routine, months-old merge step, not new infra).
incidents.what_was_built_instead: The agent ran `spacedock merge guard --verdict passed` (which only "arms" the entity for merge) and then, instead of continuing straight through to construct and push the PR, drifted into approving a DIFFERENT entity's (sc5) CI reruns and writing a full session debrief. When the captain caught the gap ("wait, i thought dp was PR'ed and ci approved?"), the agent produced the correct PR draft but then asked a third redundant confirmation instead of just executing, triggering an all-caps rebuke.
incidents.trigger_detail: The pr-merge hook's own guardrail ("present the draft to the captain... wait for explicit approval before pushing") was over-applied to an instruction already given twice, reproducing a contract gap the previous session's own handoff had named almost verbatim ("merge-guard-arm-not-a-stopping-point") — the agent's own words: "I just reproduced the first one almost exactly."
incidents.cost: ~20-message detour (ordinals ~1020-1057) at the tail of a 616-message / 433,499-output-token / ~38.5h session; delayed dp's actual push by one full debrief-writing cycle.
incidents.how_caught: Captain's direct question ("wait, i thought dp was PR'ed and ci approved?") surfaced the gap; under further challenge the agent traced it back to the handoff's already-named contract gaps.

I ALREADY SAID PUSH DP AND APPROVE CI
incidents.in_session_remediation: Agent apologized, diagnosed the "armed ≠ stopping point" pattern precisely, then executed push → PR #491 → CI approval → watched the run to actual completion ("not stopping at 'approved'... not treating 'armed' or 'opened' as a place to drift away this time"). No structural contract fix landed in-session beyond this self-diagnosis; the gap was flagged as still-open, having now recurred across two consecutive sessions.

verdict.reasoning: Transcript checks out almost verbatim, but the analyst's framing as "unasked-for/over-engineered work" does not fit what actually happened, and "permission already given twice" undersells it — it was given at least twice plus a third all-caps repeat. Spine: ordinal 566 captain says "dispatch dp ideation with opus. approve sc5." (dp's line starts here); ordinal 960 dp's validation cycle 4 comes back PASSED; ordinal 968 captain says "push it" (referring to dp — agent itself confirms: "This is dp's first terminal boundary this session"); ordinal 971 captain says "approve its CI. debrief." The agent only ran `spacedock merge guard --verdict passed` (arming, not pushing), then read the ambiguous "its" as sc5/PR#490 (the only entity with an actually-open PR at that moment — a defensible, reasoned interpretation given dp had no PR yet, not an invented task), approved sc5's pending CI reruns (continuing captain-authorized sc5 work from ordinal 566/652), and wrote the debrief the captain had just explicitly asked for ("debrief."). Captain caught the gap at 1025 ("wait, i thought dp was PR'ed and ci approved?"), repeated the instruction at 1027, and after the agent showed the PR draft again instead of executing, sent the all-caps rebuke at 1038. Agent then executed push→PR#491→CI-approval→watched to completion at 1039-1057, matching the claim's remediation description almost word for word. Cost figures verified via SQL against the sessions table: message_count=616, total_output_tokens=433499, started_at 2026-07-08T12:47:35Z, ended_at 2026-07-10T03:12:30Z = ~38.4h — all match the claim closely, and the ordinal range ~1020-1057 for the detour is accurate. However, the core allegation category is wrong: nothing here was "unasked-for" or "over-engineered." Every action taken — pushing dp, approving CI (whether sc5's or dp's), and writing a debrief — had been explicitly requested by the captain earlier in the same session (566, 971). No unauthorized infrastructure, feature, or scope was built; the agent did not invent extra work. The actual defect is a communication/interpretation failure (an ambiguous pronoun applied to the wrong entity, compounded by mistaking "armed" for "pushed") plus one redundant confirmation step before executing an instruction already given twice — a process-compliance/guardrail-application problem, not scope creep or over-engineering. So while the incident itself is real and well-corroborated (including the agent's own precise self-diagnosis linking it to a named prior-session contract gap), it should not be filed under "unasked-for/over-engineered work" — the work was fully authorized, just delayed and momentarily misdirected. Severity is contained: roughly 20 messages out of a 616-message/38.5h session, no infrastructure needed reverting, the agent self-corrected once confronted, and dp landed as PR #491 with CI approved before session end.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against the transcript of 5543d152-838b-4919-8e55-c9dacdcf0496 and against git history; the claim holds up, with one factual overstatement worth correcting.

Authorization check: the only captain message near the trigger is ordinal 128, "are theese two same underlying issue?" — a plain factual question, not a request for orchestration. The one earlier related instruction (ordinal 11, "intake issue 484 and 485 into 0250 sprint, and dispatch ideation with fable") only authorized the ideation+independent-staff-review pipeline that had already run (ordinals 100-126) — it does not cover this separate follow-up fact-check. No message anywhere in the session authorizes a Workflow-tool/multi-agent dispatch for this specific question. The agent dispatched `[Tool: Workflow]` at ordinal 129 unprompted (ordinal 131: "Workflow running in the background to verify the code-level relationship precisely"). The captain caught it immediately at ordinal 132: "i thought we just merged a change that encourage the simplest approach. why are you using a 2-subagent workflow for a small check? let it finish and run self-diagnose." The agent's ordinal-133 self-diagnosis matches the analyst's summary verbatim in substance, and ordinal 135 answers the same question directly with grep, confirming the mechanism was unnecessary for the literal question asked.

Contract-timing check (verifies the captain's premise, not just the agent's compliance): commit 3ef1ad45 "FO smallest-sufficient-mechanism gate — stop spurious orchestration / busywork (#478)" merged 2026-07-07 12:36 local, and this session started 2026-07-07 22:52 UTC the same day — the captain's "we just merged a change" claim is accurate, not a misremembering.

Cost sanity check: sessions table confirms message_count=361, total_output_tokens=299989 for this session — the claim's figures are exact, not exaggerated. Backlog filing at ordinal 317 (`spacedock new smallest-sufficient-mechanism-deterministic-fact-gate ...`) is confirmed as described — a small, proportionate governance note, not overbuilt infra requiring reversion.

One correction to the analyst's narrative: the agent did not "abort" the Workflow approach. At ordinal 133 it explicitly states "Not killing the running workflow since it's in flight — letting it finish per your instruction," per the captain's own "let it finish" directive. The workflow completed in the background (ordinal 136) and, notably, surfaced one genuine additional material gap (state sweep routes through a third, separate resolver implementation) that neither the direct grep check, the original ensign, nor the independent staff reviewer had caught — so the dispatch wasn't entirely valueless, just unrequested and disproportionate to the literal question asked.

Net: this is a real, well-evidenced incident of unrequested/disproportionate orchestration, self-identified and captain-corrected within two turns, with accurate cost figures and a proportionate remediation (a backlog note, not new infrastructure). Severity is low: contained to one dispatch, caught immediately, no lasting artifact to maintain or revert.

remedies.name: Smallest sufficient mechanism (both directions)
remedies.intent: Before the FO climbs to a workflow, dispatched worker, or PR — or re-runs verification a stage already owns — it must name in one line why the cheaper rung cannot do it; climbing is justified only by fan-out, isolation, or independent adversarial verification.
remedies.efficacy: Wording-present-only for the observed incidents. It explicitly exempts the commissioned path ('Commissioned workflow dispatch is mandatory... in-house execution is not a lower rung'), so inside a running workflow — where all three projects' incidents happened — it governs nothing. It constrains the FO's choice of dispatch mechanism, never the ensign's deliverable content (a PTY harness is worker-side content, invisible to this rule). The one-line justification is self-attested prose: no gate, AC scan, or binary ever checks it. By the contract's own standard ('a prose-only rule's ceiling is: the wording is present'), this rule fails its own bar.

remedies.name: Mechanism-to-value re-anchor in «gate.ac-cross-check»
remedies.intent: A mechanism-only AC ('the section rewritten', 'the verb shipped') passes only when the value-measuring AC it serves is also satisfied; explicitly, 'a leaner-contract entity whose contract GREW is a REJECT'. This is the contract's one genuinely anti-bloat gate device.
remedies.efficacy: Conditionally real but usually dormant. Its own guard says it 'bites only when' a paired value-measuring AC exists — and ACs are authored in the same ideation stage by the same crew, with nothing requiring a cost/leanness/proportionality AC. 'Built comprehensive PTY test harness' as a mechanism AC with no paired value AC sails through unexamined. Would not have bitten in any of the three observed incidents unless the captain had hand-authored a leanness AC first.

remedies.name: AC evidence discipline (citation per AC, external-proof bar)
remedies.intent: Every AC needs an evidence citation from a check outside the entity's own prose; an AC 'whose only proof is review of the entity's own prose' is a REJECT. Aimed at vacuous, self-referential completion claims.
remedies.efficacy: One-sided, and therefore backfires. It verifies only the PASSING direction — 'here is the run that proves it' is a green run; nothing in the FO loop, gate flow, or AC scan ever requires observing the failing/negative case (the only negative-case language in the system is the opt-in 'live scenario' discipline in the dev template). A tautological test that always passes is fully satisfying evidence under this rule, and the ensign report protocol ('Do not paste full test output — 5/5 passed is sufficient', ensign-shared-core.md:85) guarantees the gate never sees the test content. Net effect: the rule creates demand for citable tests while being structurally blind to their vacuity.

remedies.name: Present-gate pedantry tiering (Material/Polish + rule 7 'No format-pedantry asides')
remedies.intent: Reviewer findings render in two tiers; format drift 'is not load-bearing for a gate decision'; Polish is non-blocking and dropped when empty.
remedies.efficacy: Real but narrow: it governs how the FO RENDERS findings to the captain, not how findings are DISPOSITIONED. It only de-fangs format/wording pedantry. A substantively-correct edge case (the symlink finding) classifies as Material ('fact-corrections... claims contradicted by the codebase') and the contract offers no 'correct but disproportionate for this codebase's maturity' verdict — the sanctioned outcomes are fix-now via feedback routing or file-a-followup, both of which ARE the incident.

remedies.name: Feedback cycle-3 escalation
remedies.intent: Track '### Feedback Cycles'; on cycle 3, escalate to the human instead of another rework round — bounds reviewer/implementer ping-pong.
remedies.efficacy: Bounds only RUNAWAY loops. Two full cycles of pedantic rework are contract-legal before any human sees it, and the observed incidents were cycle-1 over-compliance (agent simply did what the reviewer said), which this never touches.

remedies.name: «dispatch.checklist» cap: ≤3 linchpins, no padding
remedies.intent: Dispatch checklist is at most three outcome signals; 'do not pad'; 'name what separates a good outcome from a ceremonial one' — explicitly anti-ceremony at the dispatch artifact.
remedies.efficacy: Real at its layer and probably the healthiest clause in the contract, but its layer is thin: it caps what the FO ASKS for, not what the ensign BUILDS to satisfy a signal. 'Smoke test passes end-to-end' is one compliant linchpin that an ensign can legally satisfy with a full PTY harness.

remedies.name: Single-entity bounded scope + one-workflow «engage» scope
remedies.intent: A headless run naming one entity scopes all work to that entity, runs to a bounded stop condition, and shuts workers down; «engage» converges exactly one workflow per invocation.
remedies.efficacy: Genuine containment WHEN the session is launched that way. Interactive sessions and ordinary engage loops — where the flake-to-4-PRs drift occurred — have no equivalent bound; nothing caps how many followup entities or PRs one investigation may spawn inside a legal event loop.

remedies.name: Opt-in proof disciplines + 'high-stakes surfaces' scoping
remedies.intent: Test-first authoring, external-proof ACs, detached adversarial audit, and live-scenario proof are 'recommended dev-shape practices, not universal — adopt the ones the mission needs'; adversarial audit is scoped to high-stakes surfaces (launchers, guard paths, CI/release machinery).
remedies.efficacy: This is the ONLY proportionality lever in the entire system, and it is (a) a one-time commission-time choice buried mid-template, (b) workflow-wide — once folded into the validation stage every entity gets the same bar with no per-entity dial, and (c) subordinate to the boot-resident code-gate rule, which applies at full strength regardless of what was opted out. Its live-scenario clause contains the system's only negative-case ('a negative case that reds the grade') anti-tautology requirement — opt-in, dev-template-only.

remedies.name: FO self-evidence bar ('Hold your own gate... to the bar you impose on workers')
remedies.intent: No fake greens: a skipped/cancelled check is not a pass, 'the absence of a red is not the presence of a green', failures are read from this run's evidence rather than an inherited 'known flake' label.
remedies.efficacy: Marginal as a remedy (it polices check EXECUTION, not check CONTENT — a vacuous green satisfies it completely) and net-negative for scope: its flake clause ('a relevant check that flakes is re-run to green (serial, isolated), never skipped'; the known-flake label 'is a hypothesis to confirm against this run') mandates unbounded per-run flake investigation with no file-and-move-on disposition. The flake-to-4-PRs incident is this clause operating as written — see active_drivers.

active_drivers: 'Prefer a code gate over a prose-only rule' (first-officer-shared-core.md:164): 'if the guarantee matters, the real assurance is a code-level gate underneath' and an AC 'is satisfied only by: the binary or a test enforces X, and here is the run that proves it'. Unscoped by project maturity or cost, this is a standing instruction to convert any guarantee that 'matters' into enforcement code — for a zellij-plugin prototype the only way to make TUI behavior executable evidence is a PTY harness (incident class 1), and the clause's named preferred forms ('a status guard', a failing test) are exactly gate/guard machinery (class 2).

Gate REJECT on missing/prose-only evidence (first-officer-shared-core.md:88 'an AC with no evidence whose natural place was this stage is a REJECT'; :164 'the AC cross-check refuses a criterion whose only proof is review of the entity's own prose'): at the gate, absent executable evidence bounces the entity back to implementation, whose cheapest compliant response is to author a test that passes. Since only the passing run is ever verified, this is direct selection pressure FOR tautological tests (class 3) — the contract manufactures the demand and never audits the supply.

Ensign proof rules (ensign-shared-core.md:26-28): 'Prove by exercising, not by re-reading... A substring search is not proof of behavior' plus 'No hidden machine dependencies... Anything needed to run or verify must be declared and present in the repo'. For interactive/terminal deliverables, 'running the behavior and observing the outcome' implies terminal automation, and the repo-presence rule pushes that harness INTO the repo as committed infrastructure instead of a throwaway local check (classes 1 and 2).

The flake clause of the FO self-evidence bar (first-officer-shared-core.md:167-169): 'a relevant check that flakes is re-run to green (serial, isolated), never skipped' and a prior 'known flake' label is only 'a hypothesis to confirm against this run'. No depth bound, no cost ceiling, no sanctioned 'file it and move on' path — the one-flake-investigation-to-4-open-PRs incident is this clause plus keep-moving executing as designed (class 5).

Keep-moving cadence + 'not a stopping point' (first-officer-shared-core.md:174-177 and :76): 'advance and dispatch the next stage before yielding... want me to advance + dispatch? is the violation'; 'independent followups to file + ideate' dispatch in parallel; a completed non-gated stage MUST be advanced before the turn ends. This removes the natural pause where a human would cap scope, and names followup-filing as sanctioned parallel work — the approved disposition for a byproduct finding is MORE entities and PRs. Its own guard defers to the smallest-sufficient-mechanism gate, which exempts commissioned dispatch, i.e., no teeth precisely where it matters (class 5).

'Do obvious reversible work without ceremony' + 'Don't ask permission for a step the contract already allows' (first-officer-shared-core.md:160,183): adding a CI workflow file, an approval mod, or a test harness is reversible work the contract nowhere reserves to the captain, so no one asks (class 2).

Present-gate Material tier definition (present-gate/SKILL.md:39): Material includes 'fact-corrections, contract violations, missing AC evidence, claims contradicted by the codebase' — any technically-correct reviewer edge case (the symlink case) classifies as Material and therefore gate-blocking-by-default, with fix-now or file-a-followup as the only exits (class 4).
gaps: No rigor/maturity dial anywhere — confirmed by grep across the whole 0.26.0-pre1 skills tree (zero hits for rigor/maturity/proportional/dial; 'prototype' appears nowhere). No frontmatter field, stage property, or boot-record key can express 'this is a prototype/spike', so the code-gate rule, AC evidence discipline, and validation stage apply at full strength to disposable code. The commission-time opt-in proof disciplines are the sole lever, workflow-wide and invisible after commissioning.

No non-vacuity check on tests: the entire evidence discipline verifies the passing run only. Nothing ever requires observing the failing/negative case except the opt-in live-scenario clause in the dev template. A test that cannot fail is first-class AC evidence.

The report protocol actively hides test content from the gate: 'Do not paste full test output — 5/5 passed is sufficient' (ensign-shared-core.md:85) means the FO and captain judge test evidence by count, making tautological tests undetectable at the gate by design.

No disposition for 'correct but not worth it': reviewer findings can be fixed, tiered Polish (format-only), or filed as followups. There is no decline verdict for a substantively-correct-but-disproportionate finding short of the captain manually overriding at a gate.

Smallest-sufficient-mechanism is unverified and self-exempting: no gate, scan, or binary checks the one-line justification, and the clause disclaims the commissioned path. The contract's own thesis — 'a prose-only rule's ceiling is: the wording is present' — applies to every one of its anti-over-engineering guards; all of them are prose-only, while its pro-verification rules get shipped binaries (--ac-scan, --checklist, context-budget, reconcile).

No cost/effort accounting: no clause ever asks what a stage cost relative to its value. The only 'budget' in the system is the context-token probe for worker reuse. Nothing would flag 4 PRs from one flake, or a harness larger than the prototype it tests, as anomalous.

No cap or captain checkpoint on entity/PR fan-out: filing followups is named as sanctioned parallel work (keep-moving), with no threshold that forces surfacing 'this investigation has spawned N units' before dispatching them.
remedies.notes: The contract is engineered almost exclusively against UNDER-verification — vacuous prose proofs, fake greens, self-approval, premature reaping, stalling between stages. Every shipped code mechanism (status --ac-scan, --checklist, dispatch build, context-budget, reconcile) serves evidence-production or momentum; every anti-over-engineering guard is prose-only, and two of the four (smallest-sufficient-mechanism, mechanism-to-value re-anchor) carry explicit self-exemptions or dormancy guards. The observed incidents are therefore mostly NOT agents violating the contract — classes 1 (PTY harness), 3 (tautological tests), and 5 (flake to 4 PRs) are the contract executing as written on projects whose maturity it cannot see, and class 3 is partially CAUSED by the evidence discipline's one-sided verification plus the report rule that hides test content. Two asymmetries worth quoting back to the parent: (a) the contract diagnoses its own weakness ('a prose-only rule's ceiling is: the wording is present') yet ships all restraint rules as prose while shipping all rigor rules as binaries; (b) 'Prefer a code gate over a prose-only rule' is a ratchet with no counter-ratchet — there is no 'prefer no gate over a gate nobody needs'. Also relevant context: the user-level CLAUDE.md active in these sessions (mandatory TDD for every feature/bugfix, 'Tests MUST comprehensively cover ALL functionality', 'Fix broken things immediately when you find them') compounds classes 1, 3, and 5 for any ensign that inherits it — the two rule systems reinforce each other with no proportionality escape in either. Key files: first-officer-shared-core.md (Working Principles block, lines 162-184, is the load-bearing section), ensign-shared-core.md lines 24-28, present-gate/SKILL.md rules 4/6/7, feedback-rejection-flow/SKILL.md step 3, commission/references/templates/development.md lines 88-97.

No propagation loop from evolved READMEs back into the template: spacedock-v1's mechanism-to-value trace, zaphod's interactive/offline AC split, and the materiality taxonomy are template-worthy post-incident inventions that exist only where the incident already happened. Refit updates scaffolding versions, not learned policy.

Proportionality rules are prose-only everywhere: only the tautology bans have partial code/config gates (contractlint detector, roborev test-proof-gate + output rule). Nothing mechanically detects an unasked coordination layer, enforces the 90-minute stop, or gates infra addition.

Validation/review checklists lack a small-change fast path in all three READMEs — the natural home would be a diff-size or blast-radius tier mirroring the detached-audit's 'routine changes exempt' clause, applied to the whole validation Output list.

Natural homes for the missing declarations exist and are already scaffolded: the template's '## Workflow-specific rules' section (workflow-level posture: maturity, default test depth, infra-addition policy, review-finding priority), per-stage Good/Bad bullets (stage-level realization — the established pattern), the commission interview (a maturity question feeding both), and .roborev.toml review_guidelines (the proven config surface that mechanically reaches reviewers).

active_drivers: The 'semantic adversarial pass' — now duplicated verbatim in .roborev.toml (lines 24-32) AND the docs/dev/README.md validation diff (new lines 139-144) — is a pedantry GENERATOR: it instructs the reviewer/validator to build a matrix of Unicode/EOF/size/visibility/layout boundary variants and to 'add one scaling or over-limit test when that risk exists' during validation. The classification tiers exist precisely to mop up what this pass produces; running it in a prototype context manufactures the symlink-edge-case class of finding.

Roborev's own verdict mechanics: any entry under '## Review Findings' fails the job, 'roborev wait' exits 1 on a failed verdict, and 'roborev refine' is an 'iterative review-fix loop until all reviews pass' — a code-level driver of dutiful fixing that the remedies can only steer by controlling what lands under that heading. The roborev-setup draft bans refine/agent-hook in Spacedock workflows for exactly this reason, but that ban is unshipped.

The Test proof gate (.roborev.toml lines 16-22) auto-escalates test-strength findings to 'a Material evidence defect even when another test covers the happy path' on a very broad surface list (any 'required acceptance, release, CI, compatibility, or detached-audit surface'), partially undoing the release-scope triage for test findings.

'Classification ... never suppresses a real observation' plus mandatory non-blocking reporting of every deferred risk keeps pedantic findings continuously in front of agents that have no consumption rule for them.

The user-global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md pushes workers hard toward fixing every reported finding: 'Tests MUST comprehensively cover ALL functionality', 'ALL TEST FAILURES ARE YOUR RESPONSIBILITY', 'Fix broken things immediately when you find them', 'NEVER skip steps or take shortcuts' — an ensign holding both this and a reviewer finding has no licensed way to not fix it.

spacedock-subspace's post-commit hook panel (hook_review_panel = 'quick') reviews every commit, generating a continuous finding stream; its instructions carry the Material-only output rule, but the hook itself guarantees pedantry has a delivery channel on every commit.
gaps: No ensign-side consumption rule anywhere: /Users/clkao/git/spacedock-research/spacedock-v1/skills/ensign/references/ensign-shared-core.md contains zero guidance on triaging review findings before fixing them. The exact actor in the incident class — the ensign that dutifully fixes a symlink edge case — is the one actor no remedy addresses. Every remedy sits upstream (reviewer output shaping) or downstream (validator/FO gate, captain presentation).

No re-triage on misclassification: if the reviewer model ignores the output rule and puts a deferred risk under '## Review Findings', the verdict fails, and nothing in feedback-rejection-flow or the FO contract requires checking that a REJECTED/failing verdict cites a material finding before routing fix work. The whole design rides on one prose hop at generation.

The classification is not machine-readable: material-vs-deferred exists only as markdown-heading placement in the reviewer's narrative. Roborev has severity (--min-severity) but no release-scope field, no schema, and no lint verifying the four-field triage was performed — the config even has to explain roborev's failure semantics to the reviewer ('Roborev treats every entry there as a failure').

The two live-fire pieces are not committed: spacedock-v1/.roborev.toml is untracked (absent from worktrees where implementation ensigns run branch reviews; one 'git clean' from gone) and the docs/dev/README.md validation-stage classification is an unstaged diff (dispatched fresh validators reading committed state see the OLD text). Only subspace's config and the present-gate/feedback-rejection-flow skills are actually deployed.
Deferred risks have no afterlife: promotion conditions are recorded in prose summaries but no mechanism (entity field, backlog task, tracker query) ever revisits them.

The semantic adversarial pass and the release-scope triage text are now triplicated (v1 toml, subspace toml, README) with divergent wording — drift risk, and the README copy turns a reviewer calibration into a validator work instruction (including 'add one scaling test'), re-importing pedantry into the workflow stage the triage was meant to protect.

The agent-collaboration spec's core protections (audience separation, signed outward request) are unimplemented, and the spec itself records that the Subspace TUI still fails to resolve References into readable views — so today a maintainer steering a review sees raw JSON, the condition under which the PR #511 leak happened.

No prototype/maturity signal reaches the reviewer: the v1 config asserts 'compatibility-first' posture repo-wide; nothing lets a task or entity declare 'this is a spike/prototype — apply deferred-risk defaults', so the reviewer must infer maturity per-diff.
remedies.notes: Design summary: the in-flight remedy is a classification-and-routing scheme, not a suppression scheme. It defines four finding classes (Material / Deferred risk / Polish / Needs decision) with a mandatory four-field evidence record (released user+workflow, observable harm, violated AC/boundary, trigger evidence), decouples severity from release scope, and then exploits roborev's verdict mechanics: since roborev fails a job on any '## Review Findings' entry, the config's output rule ('put ONLY material findings ... there') converts the prose classification into an exit-code difference. That is the actual answer to 'what stops an ensign from dutifully fixing a pedantic finding': when it works, the ensign never receives a blocking signal, because the finding was born non-blocking. The second intervention point is the workflow gate: the README diff makes 'only material findings block the gate or consume a feedback cycle' the validator's recommendation rule, which matters because REJECTED is the trigger for spacedock:feedback-rejection-flow — so it is genuinely wired into the loop, not config-only. The third (present-gate tiers) shapes captain decisions only, and the fourth (the collaboration spec) is an unimplemented future design for cross-agent PR review whose key idea is that a contributor's agent only ever receives a human-signed atomic change request. Overall assessment: intervention is heavily front-loaded at review generation (prose-compliance-dependent, and the v1 copy is untracked), moderately present at the FO gate (unstaged diff), and entirely absent at the ensign — the fix-executing agent has no triage license, while the global CLAUDE.md actively instructs it to fix everything. The cheapest high-leverage completions would be: commit the two in-flight files; add a 3-4 line triage clause to ensign-shared-core.md; and add an FO check in feedback-rejection-flow that routed findings name their material classification.
